title: Saving Salvage's crashed, nearly new Audi RS3 is rebuilt, and its chassis escaped

verdict: Probably yes, though not by much that we can prove. The builder's gamble paid off where it counted most: the description says the main chassis components were unscathed, so this became a panels-and-paint job, not a structural rebuild [3]. A clean nearly new RS3 still lists around £64,000 (about $85,000) in the UK [4]. A disclosed-crash car worth $58,000 to $72,000 leaves room for profit, but only if the unstated purchase price was well below that. The build shows why buying privately, before an insurer categorises the car, is attractive to rebuilders. It also shows the risk: nobody knew what was hidden underneath.
body:
## The buy

Saving Salvage, the UK channel that has rebuilt two earlier generations of Audi RS3 on camera, went newer this summer. In a video posted on July 22, 2026, titled "I BOUGHT A £72,000 2026 BRAND NEW CRASHED AUDI RS3!", the channel showed a nearly new, crashed RS3 [1]. The £72,000 (about $95,800) in the title is the car's value when new, not the price paid. No purchase price appears in the title or description, so this file leaves the price blank [1].

This was not a salvage-auction buy. The description says the car came from a subscriber, and the channel admitted there was no guarantee it could be fixed [1]. The description also says the car "hasnt been through an insurance assessment" [1]. That matters in Britain. An insurer's assessment is what puts a car on the record as a Category S (structural) or Category N (non-structural) write-off. A car that skips the assessment may carry no write-off marker at all. We could not confirm the car's status on the register, so the title field here reads "unknown" rather than "salvage." If it had been categorised, Cat S or Cat N would map to "salvage" in our terms.

## The damage

When he bought it, the builder did not know how badly the car was hurt. He also did not know whether it ran [1]. By the second episode, on July 30, most of the damaged panels were off. The description says it was "time to start ordering parts and working out how much this is going to cost to fix", and notes he still had to check for hidden damage [2].

The finale, posted October 21, gives the answer. Looking back, the builder writes that the car "was in a really bad shape on the surface" but that underneath "the main chassis components got away completely unscathed" [3]. That is the outcome every crash rebuilder hopes for: bent metal you can see, and no damage to the suspension mounts, subframes or structure. Those are the repairs that cost real money and drag a job out. The channel's descriptions don't say which corner took the hit, and we haven't guessed.

## The work and the parts

The episodes we could check name no part numbers or invoices. The parts list on this page therefore stays general, with costs left blank where nobody has published a figure. The work follows the channel's usual pattern. It strips the damage, prices the parts (the PT2 description links the AUTODOC parts store with a viewer discount code), fixes or refurbishes the wheels (the same description links JR Alloy Wheel Repair), then reassembles and paints [2]. The purchase episode's description also links OBDeleven, the Audi-group diagnostic and coding tool. Coding is usually needed once crash sensors or modules have been replaced [1].

From purchase video to finale the build took about three months on camera, July 22 to October 21, 2026. The finale says the car was bought "2 months ago" [3]. That probably counts from when the work was filmed, not when the video went up. The finale's title says it plainly: "I FULLY REBUILT THIS MANGLED BRAND NEW AUDI RS3!" [3].

## The money

No one has published a bill, so we can't give a profit figure. What we can do is set the market around it. All pound figures here are converted at about $1.33 to the pound.

- New, the channel puts the car at £72,000 (about $95,800) [1].
- At the main-dealer end, a 2025 RS3 Carbon Vorsprung saloon with 4,211 miles was listed by Stafford Audi as an Audi Approved Used car at £63,980, about $85,100, and has since sold or been withdrawn [4].
- In the U.S., where the RS3 lists for less (autoevolution gives $66,100 for a 2026 [6]), Classic.com tracked a 2026 RS3 with about 3,000 miles last asking $69,186 and a 2025 with about 4,000 miles at $62,990, both in October 2026 [5]. A 2025 RS3 bought new for $77,990 was bid only to $50,000 on Cars & Bids a week before the end of its October 2025 auction, with under 2,900 miles on it [6]. Nearly new RS3s lose value quickly.

Then comes the history discount. AUTODOC's UK guide says Cat S cars typically lose 20 to 50% against undamaged equivalents, and suggests expecting about 30% less [7]. If this car carries no category, the discount should be smaller, but a buyer who has watched the crash on YouTube will still knock money off. Taking the £63,980 dealer car as the clean benchmark and cutting 15 to 30% gives about £44,800 to £54,400, or roughly $58,000 to $72,000.

## What's next

The finale says the car is fully rebuilt, so this file marks it finished. Nothing we found shows it for sale or sold. If the channel keeps it, a long-term video should show how a crash-repaired, out-of-warranty-risk RS3 holds up. If it sells, the asking price and whether the advert declares a category will settle what the gamble earned. We'll also look for the purchase price, which has not been stated yet.
